title: The Importance of Celebration and Rest for Creatives
content:
The Importance of Celebration and Rest for Creative Work

In an industry obsessed with the next big thing, sometimes the wisest move is to chill out and celebrate the little things.

It’s been a year. And when I say that, I mean it’s been a year.

You look away for just a moment and suddenly there’s a new AI model, a prompt approach, a new resolution boosting tool for human skin, then a different one for everything that’s not-human-skin, and not a single shortage of hot takes about why the way you’ve been working is already obsolete.

Point blank, keeping up sucks.

I say that as a brand designer, who loves my craft and who is so damn thankful for generative fill its unreal. My work sits at the exact intersection of taste, craft, scale, and all this constant change (not to mention the moral dilemmas stopping at that intersection.)

Brand work has scale, it’s technical, and it’s strategic. There is always another surface to consider, another pattern to set, another product launch to support, another marketing narrative to thread in, and another stakeholder to align with. We’re constantly moving. Over the past year, though, I’ve felt how important it is to have real deadlines to celebrate, and real moments of rest and to slow down.

Because without them, the work, and the people doing it, slowly wither away.

1. Moving the finish line is demotivating

Listen, creative work is never truly done done. Ideas evolve. Systems mature. Context shifts. That’s normal. But when every milestone becomes negotiable, when “we’ll just push it a bit” turns into the default, two subtle but dangerous realities become true:

  • Your team is always pouring out and never rewarded by shipping their work. (*nudge nudge* that’s likely the reason we all got into the industry in the first place.)
  • The very real excuse of ‘oh, we’ll just push it again’ fiendishly erodes the expectations and lowers the bar for the quality of work.

You ship what feels like your best thinking, clear, considered, hard-won, only for it to be immediately overruled by the a newer set of requirements, the next insight, or the latest priority reshuffle. There’s no ceremony to mark the moment. No closure. Just a quiet slide into the next ‘sprint’.

David Ogilvy famously believed in respecting the work enough to finish it. Not endlessly polish it into oblivion, not constantly reopen it out of fear, but ship it with conviction. I love to say this at work, “We’re marketers, not Michelangelo.” There’s a difference, hunny. In creative work, deadlines aren’t just operational — they are psychological. They force clarity. They create pride.

Solution? Begin with the end in mind, set SMART goals as an org. If there is too much complexity to manage, break it down to smaller steps. Do one thing at a time. Trust me that makes it so much easier collecting stakeholder input and then their feedback too.

2. Retros are where meaning gets made and teams get stronger

Creatives live for the grand reveal. For the case study. For that flick-of-a-switch brand moment that goes live at midnight and suddenly exists in the world. I hunch that’s why we as a larger group of marketing professionals all put in the hours of strategy and focus too; to put work out into the world for other humans to experience. That pressure, that pride, is why we obsess over kerning most won’t notice and why copywriters debate the exact right phrasing of the idea. It’s why we (politely, passionately) argue about edge cases and ‘what ifs’. It’s because the work is going out into the world and that’s the payoff.

But celebration doesn’t just mean smashing the rocket ship emoji in Slack.

It means retros where we actually reflect. Team moments that name what was hard, what worked, what surprised you. It means saying, out loud, “That was ambitious, and we pulled it off.” At Config 2025 in San Francisco, this came up repeatedly: the best design orgs aren’t just high-output machines. They’re meaning-making systems. They slow down on purpose to look back before they look ahead.

Without those moments, teams don’t grow closer, nor do they bond by their experiences; they just survive the next delivery.

3. Rest is not a reward. It’s a creative input.

I’ll say it again. Rest is not the reward. It’s the mandatory creative gasoline in the tank.

Noticing how real-life shadows fall and catch light. Seeing a random piece of signage that solves the same problem you’ve been wrestling with for a while. Walking into a store, opening an app, overhearing a conversation—suddenly, the answer clicks.

That only happens when there’s space.

Distance from work is what allows you to see it objectively. Time away from the problem almost always leads to a wiser solve. This isn’t indulgence or laziness; it’s mechanics. Your brain needs idle cycles to connect dots. Rest doesn’t make you slower. It makes you sharper.

In closing, deadlines matter because they force clarity and celebration. Retros matter because slowing down gives work and our process meaning. Rest matters because it gives your ideas room to breathe.

In an industry obsessed with the next big thing, sometimes the wisest move is to chill out and celebrate the little things.
